intro: Lazur is an AI assistant for Google Sheets on Mac that works next to your browser, not inside it. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and it answers out loud. It explains errors, points at menus, walks you through steps, and drafts text at the cursor. It does not click buttons for you.
tldr: Google Sheets has no native Mac app. You use it in a browser, and Lazur works alongside that browser.
Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask what is on screen. Lazur answers out loud and circles the item you ask about.
Hold fn to dictate text at the cursor. Ask Lazur to draft a note and it types the text where your cursor sits.
Lazur explains and points. It does not click for you, so every change to your data stays with you.
Google raised the cell limit to 20 million cells per file, but many guides still show the old figure.

blocks.text: What Lazur does inside Google Sheets on Mac

Google Sheets runs in your browser, so Lazur does not live inside the sheet. It lives in the notch at the top of your Mac and watches the screen while you hold the shortcut. You keep working in the sheet. You ask questions out loud, and the answer comes back without a copy and paste into a chat window.
Five jobs cover most of what you will ask. Lazur explains, points, guides, drafts, and dictates. Each one answers a different kind of question.

items: Explain: read an error, a formula, or a warning and say what it means in plain words.
Point: circle a menu, a tool, or a cell so you know where to look.
Guide: walk through a feature one click at a time, waiting for each click.
Draft: write a note, a label, or a short reply and type it where your cursor sits.
Dictate: hold fn and speak. Clean, formatted text lands at the cursor in any app.

blocks.text: Lazur does not click for you. When it guides you, it waits for each click from you. That is slower than a macro. It also means you see every change before it happens.
Why Google Sheets on Mac runs in a browser

There is no native Google Sheets app for Mac. Google describes Sheets as a browser app. Its system requirements ask you to use one of the two most recent browser versions, with cookies and JavaScript turned on. Drive for desktop is a separate sync app, and it needs macOS Ventura 13.0 or higher.

That changes how you get help. The menus sit inside a browser window, and Mac shortcuts differ from Windows keys. Lazur reads the page you have open. Ask about Format > Number, and the answer matches the browser and layout you have in front of you.
How big a Google Sheets file can get

File size decides whether a sheet works at all. Google's Workspace Updates post says the cell limit rose from up to 10 million cells to up to 20 million cells. The change covers new, existing, and imported files. The rollout began in September 2026.

Google's Drive help page lists the same limit, up to 20 million cells or 100MB, for spreadsheets created in or converted to Google Sheets. Many older guides still say 10 million. Check the date on any guide before you trust its numbers.

Two other limits catch people. When an Excel file converts, any cell with more than 50,000 characters is removed. Connected Sheets pivot tables are capped at 200,000 rows, so check the row count before you trust the totals. Google's pages do not say whether blank cells or extra tabs count toward the cell limit. Test your file before you assume it fits.
Where people get stuck in Google Sheets

Google does not publish a ranking of the most common Sheets problems. Its help center is organized by topic. Two of those topics are Shortcuts & troubleshooting and Improve Sheets performance, which shows where trouble tends to land. The list below comes from those topics and one outside survey. Read it as a map of common trouble, not a usage count.

The best outside number is a 2022 survey of 1,001 office workers in Australia, the UK, and the US. ThoughtSpot commissioned it, and it covered spreadsheets in general, not Sheets alone. It found that 70% do not consider themselves advanced or masters of spreadsheets. The press release headline says almost half struggle to make sense of spreadsheet data, while the body gives 40% on average. If you quote it, quote the body and name the survey.

items: Errors while editing, such as 'Can't save your changes.'
Slow sheets full of lookups and data references.
Files too large to edit, or pivots that stop at a row cap.
Formulas that break after a file moves in from Excel.
Features that hide in menus, such as Data > Data validation.
Shortcuts that are hard to remember.

blocks.text: Ask what is on screen when something breaks

This is where holding the shortcut pays off. Hold ⌥ ⌘, ask your question, and let go. Lazur looks at the screen while you hold the keys, and it answers out loud. You can ask about an error in a cell, a formula in the formula bar, or a warning banner at the top of the sheet.

Say something like 'What does this error mean?' Lazur reads the message and names the likely cause. Then it suggests the next step in plain words. It will not change the cell for you. You make the change, which keeps the data in your hands.

An error that says 'Can't save your changes' needs more than a guess. The title of Google's help article for that message says to copy your recent edits, then revert your changes. Ask Lazur to walk you through the copy step. Then follow the revert step once you have a copy saved.
Google's error help lists several general fixes. Try them in this order, and stop when the error goes away.

items: Wait five minutes, then reload the page.
Open a private window to see whether an extension is the cause. In Chrome, that is ⇧ ⌘ N.
Clear the browser cache and cookies.
Check your connection, update the browser, or try another browser.
If the file is too large to edit, copy the tabs you need into a new spreadsheet.

blocks.title: Cookies reach past Sheets
blocks.text: Clearing cookies signs you out of more than Sheets. It affects the whole browser, so use it after the simpler steps have failed.
Fix a lookup that shows #N/A

A lookup that returns #N/A usually means the value it searched for is not in the range it searched. The usual causes are extra spaces, a number stored as text, or a range that starts one row too late. Ask Lazur: 'Why does this formula say N/A?' It reads the formula bar aloud and names the likely cause.

Then ask it to point at the range in the formula. Lazur circles the part you need to check. Compare the first column of the range with the value in your cell. If the names look identical but do not match, a stray space is the usual reason.
If the sheet stays slow after you fix it, Google's Improve Sheets performance topic covers optimizing data references and LOOKUP performance. Read those articles next, not a random forum post.
Point at buttons and menus without hunting

Sheets has many menus, and the names do not always match the task in your head. Google's shortcut page says the Tool finder, formerly called Search the menus, opens with Option+/ on Mac. Use it when you know the task but not the menu name.

If you would rather ask, do that. Lazur draws a circle and a label around the item on your screen. Ask 'Where do I change the number format?' and Lazur circles the Format menu, then labels Number. The menu path is Format > Number.

Pointing works best with a clear noun. 'Where is the filter?' is vague when three filter-looking icons sit on screen. 'Where is Create a filter?' is not. Name the thing you want, and Lazur has less to guess.
Walk through a feature one click at a time

Pointing shows you where something is. Guiding shows you how to finish a task. Ask Lazur to walk you through it, and it moves one click at a time. It waits for your click before it gives the next step. You learn the path while you work.

Try a chart. Select two columns of monthly totals, then ask 'Walk me through making a chart from these columns.' Lazur points you to Insert > Chart and waits for each click. If the chart type looks wrong, say so, and the next step changes to match.

blocks.title: Select the range first
blocks.text: Guided steps go faster when you select the range before you ask. Lazur can only point at what is on screen, so a visible selection saves a round of questions.

The same pattern works for filters. Data > Create a filter starts a filter on the range you pick. Our guide to [adding a filter to one range in Google Sheets on Mac](/how-to/add-a-filter-to-a-range-in-google-sheets) shows each step. For charts, the full path is in [how to make a chart in Google Sheets on Mac](/how-to/make-a-chart-in-google-sheets).
Draft text at the cursor and dictate in Sheets

Sheets has plenty of text cells. You need a label, a note, or a short reason for a number. Hold fn and speak. Lazur dictates clean, formatted text at the cursor. The same works in a cell, a comment box, or an email open in another window.

Draft works the same way, with more thinking. Ask 'Draft a two-line note that explains this total.' Lazur writes the text and types it where your cursor sits. Read it before you press Return. If the tone is wrong, ask for a shorter version, and it types the new one.

Snippets help with text you type every week. Lazur keeps snippets, a personal dictionary, and clipboard slots. Add client names and product names to the dictionary once, so dictation spells them the way you do. Put a standard footnote in a snippet, and you stop retyping it.
Dictation is quick to test. The [speaking vs typing test](/tools/speaking-vs-typing-test) shows how your speed compares. Try it in a note cell before you decide whether dictation fits your day.

blocks.text: Google's page also notes a Ctrl+Option pattern for Mac menus. Ctrl+Option+F opens the File menu. Ask Lazur to point at the menu bar when you want to confirm the pattern on your own screen.

blocks.title: Check the Mac key
blocks.text: Google's shortcut page lists Windows keys next to Mac keys. Check the key on your own Mac before you rely on it. If a shortcut does nothing, use the menu.
Mistakes people make with AI help in Sheets

items: Asking about the whole file when the question is about one cell. Name the column or select the cell first.
Clearing cookies to fix one sheet. Cookies affect the whole browser. Try the simple steps first.
Trusting a guide that still says 10 million cells. The current limit is 20 million.
Expecting Lazur to make the change. It explains and points. You make the change.
Dictating names without adding them to the dictionary. Add them first, so dictation spells them right.

blocks.text: What Lazur cannot do, and where the limits sit

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app. It runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available.

Research works differently. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs, through the Lazur for Chrome extension. Ask it to find Google's help article for an error, and it comes back with a summary and a report. Use that when you need a source, not a guess.
How Lazur handles what you say and what it sees

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. When you hold ⌥ ⌘, the audio and a screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer. Those are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Lazur keeps a memory of what you asked and did, on the Mac.

Check your own rules before you ask about client data. The screenshot shows anything visible on screen, including names and figures in other tabs. Close the tabs you do not want in the picture, then ask.

blocks.title: Clear the screen first
blocks.text: Lazur sees what is on screen while you hold the keys. Close sensitive tabs or windows before you ask a question about the sheet.
Start with one sheet and one question

Pick a sheet you already know. Ask one question you can answer yourself, so you can judge the reply. Then try one point, one guide, and one dictation. Within a session you will know whether the flow fits how you work.

Lazur has a free trial with no credit card. The trial starts when you first open the app. [Download Lazur for Mac](/download) when you are ready, and check the [pricing page](/pricing) for plans. Lazur answers out loud, so use headphones in a shared office.

faq.question: Is there a Google Sheets app for Mac?
faq.answer: No. Google Sheets runs in a browser, and Google's system requirements do not list a native Mac app. Drive for desktop syncs files to your Mac, but it is not a Sheets app. Lazur works next to the browser, so it helps in the sheet you already have open.

faq.question: Does Lazur edit my spreadsheet for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur explains what is on screen, points at menus and cells, walks you through steps one click at a time, and types drafted text when you ask. It does not click buttons or operate other apps. Every edit stays with you.

faq.question: What does holding ⌥ ⌘ do in Google Sheets?
faq.answer: Holding ⌥ ⌘ lets Lazur see your screen and hear your question. It answers out loud. Let go when you finish asking. Lazur sends the audio and screenshot to AI providers to answer, and those are not stored.

faq.question: Is Lazur part of Google Sheets or Gemini?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is a separate Mac app, and it is not a plugin or add-in for Sheets. Google's Sheets page describes Gemini features inside Sheets. Check Google's page if you want to compare what Sheets itself offers.

faq.question: Why do some guides say 10 million cells?
faq.answer: Google raised the cell limit from up to 10 million to up to 20 million for new, existing, and imported files. The rollout began in September 2026. Older guides were written before the change, so check their dates.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available.

faq.question: Can Lazur find the Google help page for my error?
faq.answer: Yes, with research. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs, through the Lazur for Chrome extension, and returns a summary and a report. Read the page yourself before you apply a fix, especially one that clears cookies.

faq.question: Does Lazur work outside Google Sheets?
faq.answer: Yes. Lazur works in any app on the Mac. This page covers Google Sheets in the browser, but the same hold, ask, and point habits carry over to other apps.
